You will learn the crontab five-field schedule, how to use crontab commands to create and manage user jobs, and how system-wide cron differs and uses directories like cron. daily. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Scheduling Tasks with Cron and At

Scheduling Tasks with Cron and At

Automate recurring jobs with cron and schedule one-off jobs with at.

Automation reduces human error and ensures routine maintenance runs on time. Cron is the standard for repeating schedules and reads crontab files to execute commands. At schedules single future commands using the atd service. Both run with a minimal environment, so absolute paths and output redirection are essential for reliable results.

In this lesson
Crontab syntax, crontab commands, system cron directories, and at scheduling.
Why it matters
Automating tasks saves time and prevents missed maintenance windows.
Practice
Add and test a one-minute cron entry that appends a timestamp to a file, then schedule an at job to write a short message.
Visual Concept
Jobs, Schedules, and Runners
Crontab
Five-field schedule plus command. Stored per-user and in system paths.
Cron Daemon
Runs jobs at the specified times and uses the minimal environment.
At & atd
Schedules a one-time command and stores it until execution.
Explore Key Topics
Crontab Syntax
Fields: minute, hour, day, month, weekday. Use wildcards, ranges, lists, and steps.
System Cron
/etc/crontab and cron.d include a user field and often call run-parts for cron.daily.
At Jobs
Use at to schedule once-only commands and manage them with atq and atrm.

screens.title: Cron and At: Purpose and Differences
screens.narratorSegment: Cron and at both automate commands, but they serve different needs. Cron is a time-based scheduler for recurring work. Use it for tasks that must run on a predictable cadence, such as daily backups, weekly reports, or hourly log rotation. At is for a single execution at a specified future time, for example scheduling a one-off script to run after a maintenance window. Understanding the difference helps you choose the right tool and avoid overcomplicating simple one-off needs with cron entries. A concrete example: use cron to run a script that appends a timestamp to a log every minute for monitoring, and use at to schedule a single message to be written five minutes from now. A common misconception is thinking at persists like cron; it does not create a recurring job. Another misconception is believing cron uses your interactive session variables; cron runs with a minimal environment so commands may fail unless you set PATH or use absolute binaries. The practical significance is reliability. If you select the wrong tool, you either risk missing a repeated job or cluttering crontab with one-off entries. As you practice, ask yourself whether the task repeats. If it does, cron is the right choice. If it does not, use at.

content.html:
Core Concept

Cron and At: Purpose and Differences

Define each tool, explain typical use cases, and surface common misconceptions.

Cron
  • Runs recurring jobs on a schedule defined in crontab.
  • Suitable for backups, rotation, and periodic maintenance.
At
  • Queues a single job to run at a specified future time.
  • Good for one-off tasks like delayed notifications or maintenance steps.
Misconceptions
Cron does not inherit your interactive environment; at does not repeat jobs. Use absolute paths and set PATH to avoid failures.
Concrete Example and Walkthrough
Cron example (every minute)
* * * * * /bin/echo "$(date) - My cron job ran!" >> /tmp/my_cron_log.txt 2>&1
At example (single run)
$ at now + 5 minutes
at> echo "This message was scheduled with at" > /tmp/at_message.txt
at>
Key Takeaway

Choose cron for repetition and at for one-off runs. Always make paths and output explicit to ensure repeatability.

screens.title: Crontab Format and Field Meaning
screens.narratorSegment: Crontab entries use five schedule fields followed by the command to run. Each field sets the allowed values for minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. A single star means every value for that field. Lists, ranges, and steps expand how you specify multiple times. For example, a line that runs at two in the morning every day looks like zero two star star star followed by the command. Another common need is every fifteen minutes, which you express with slash syntax like star slash fifteen. There are also convenience strings such as at reboot, hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly that map to common schedules. A practical example in your lab will be composing a line that appends a timestamp every minute. When you write crontab entries, keep sentences short and commands absolute. A frequent mistake is writing interactive scripts that rely on a user's shell environment. To avoid that, either set PATH at the top of the crontab file or use full paths in commands. Now look at the concrete examples and syntax table, then try composing a schedule for a maintenance task you run regularly. Which field is easiest for you to read and why?

content.html:
Definition & Syntax

Crontab Format and Field Meaning

Five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. Then the command.

Syntax Table
  • Minute: 0-59
  • Hour: 0-23
  • Day of month: 1-31
  • Month: 1-12 or names
  • Day of week: 0-7 or names (0 and 7 are Sunday)
Special characters
Asterisk for every value, comma for lists, hyphen for ranges, slash for step values.
Examples
# Run at 02:00 every day
0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup_script.sh

# Run every 15 minutes
*/15 * * * * /usr/bin/some_task --option >> /var/log/some_task.log 2>&1

# Run at reboot
@reboot /usr/local/bin/startup_task.sh
Key Takeaway

Use the five fields and special tokens to express schedules precisely. Prefer absolute paths and capture output.

screens.title: Managing User Crontab with the crontab Command
screens.narratorSegment: The crontab command is the user-facing tool to manage per-user crontab files. Use crontab -e to edit your crontab in your default editor. When you save and exit, cron installs the updated crontab without needing to restart the daemon. Use crontab -l to list your current entries and crontab -r to remove them all. Be very careful with crontab -r because it deletes without confirmation. A common safe pattern is to list and back up your current crontab before making edits. For example, crontab -l greater-than mycrontab. backup saves your current file. To add a simple one-minute test job, open crontab -e and add star star star star star followed by an absolute echo command that appends a timestamp to /tmp. After saving wait a minute to verify the file receives timestamps. If you need to restore, use crontab mycrontab. backup. When editing, ensure PATH is set if your commands are not full paths. Also redirect stdout and stderr to a log to capture errors and avoid mail spam. This workflow gives you an auditable and recoverable way to manage personal cron jobs. What backup strategy will you adopt before changing crontab?

content.html:
Process

Managing User Crontab with crontab

Edit, list, backup, and restore your crontab safely using standard commands.

Commands and Safe Steps
  • Edit: crontab -e (saves on exit)
  • List: crontab -l
  • Remove all: crontab -r (no confirmation)
  • Backup before edit: crontab -l > mycrontab.backup
  • Restore: crontab mycrontab.backup
Terminal Demo Example
# Backup current crontab
$ crontab -l > ~/mycrontab.backup

# Edit crontab
$ crontab -e
# Add line:
* * * * * /bin/echo "$(date) - My cron job ran!" >> /tmp/my_cron_log.txt 2>&1

# Verify
$ crontab -l

# If needed restore
$ crontab ~/mycrontab.backup
Common Mistake

Running crontab -r without a backup removes jobs irreversibly. Always save your crontab before making changes.

screens.title: System-wide Cron and Directory-based Jobs
screens.narratorSegment: System-wide cron entries live in files such as /etc/crontab and in /etc/cron. d. A key difference is that these files include an extra username field after the schedule so the system knows which account runs the command. For example, an entry might schedule root to run a cleanup script at three a. m. The distribution also commonly provides directories like /etc/cron. hourly, /etc/cron. daily, /etc/cron. weekly, and /etc/cron. monthly. The main system crontab typically calls run-parts on these directories to execute each executable script inside them at the appropriate interval. This makes it easy to deploy system-wide jobs: drop an executable script into cron. daily and it runs at the next daily run. When creating scripts for these directories, make them non-interactive and ensure they are executable and safe to run as the specified system user. A frequent oversight is forgetting the user field or placing non-executable files in cron directories. Also remember that scripts run with the minimal cron environment, so include full paths. Understanding these differences lets you choose whether a job belongs in a per-user crontab or as a system-wide script managed centrally. Which location will you choose for administrative tasks and why?

content.html:
System Configuration

System-wide Cron and Directory-based Jobs

How /etc/crontab and cron directories differ from user crontabs, and why the username field matters.

File examples
# /etc/crontab format includes user
# M H Dom Mon Dow User Command
0 3 * * * root /usr/bin/clean_temp_files.sh

# run-parts in /etc/crontab triggers scripts in cron.daily
25 6 * * * root run-parts /etc/cron.daily
Place executable scripts in cron.hourly or cron.daily. Ensure scripts are non-interactive and have strict permissions.
Deployment pattern
For centrally managed tasks, add scripts under /etc/cron.daily or files in /etc/cron.d. For user-specific tasks, use crontab -e.
Pro Tip

Use the username field to run commands as specific system accounts and avoid invoking sudo inside cron scripts.

screens.title: The at Command and Job Queue
screens.narratorSegment: The at command schedules a job to run once at a specified future time. It uses the atd daemon to hold and execute queued jobs. To submit a job, type at followed by a time specification such as now plus five minutes, a specific time, or a date. After pressing Enter you type the commands to run, one per line, and then press Ctrl+D to save. Use atq to list pending jobs and atrm with the job number to remove a job before it runs. A clear example: schedule at now plus ten minutes, then echo a message into a temporary file so you can verify execution. Because at jobs run with a minimal environment, use absolute paths in the commands you enter. Also remember that at jobs do not repeat, so they are not a replacement for cron when you need periodic work. A common mistake is forgetting to press Ctrl+D, which leaves the job unsaved, or using relative paths that fail when the job runs. Try scheduling a harmless at job in a lab environment and then use atq to observe its queued status. How would you cancel a job if you change your plan?

content.html:
Definition

The at Command and Job Queue

Schedule single future commands using at, then list and remove them with atq and atrm.

How to submit
$ at now + 10 minutes
at> echo "Hello from the future" > /tmp/at_message.txt
at> 

# List queued at jobs
$ atq

# Remove job 2
$ atrm 2
Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting Ctrl+D so the job is not saved.
  • Using relative paths that do not resolve when the job runs.
  • Not checking atq to confirm the job queued as expected.
Key Takeaway

At is for single-run tasks; verify queued jobs with atq and remove with atrm if plans change.

screens.title: Environment and PATH: Why Jobs Fail
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent cause of failed scheduled jobs is the minimal environment that cron and at provide. When you run a command interactively, your shell sets PATH and other variables. Scheduled jobs often run with a very small PATH and without shell initialization files. As a result, commands that work in your shell may not be found when cron runs them. The practical fixes are simple. First, use absolute paths for binaries, for example /usr/bin/Python three instead of Python three. Second, set PATH at the top of your crontab with a full list of directories you need. Third, ensure scripts source any required environment explicitly or avoid relying on interactive-only configuration. For troubleshooting, redirect stdout and stderr to a log file and inspect it after a scheduled run. A common remediation sequence is to run the command from a non-interactive shell to replicate cron, then add logging and absolute paths until errors disappear. As a concrete example, replace a failing line that calls Python three with the full path and a redirection to a log file. This approach quickly reveals missing commands and permission issues. What logging location will you use to capture cron failures on your system?

content.html:
Comparison

Environment and PATH: Why Jobs Fail

Understand differences between interactive shells and cron/at environments, and how to fix missing commands.

Interactive shell
  • Loads profile and shell rc files.
  • PATH and other variables are set for user convenience.
Cron / at environment
  • Minimal PATH and no interactive shell initialization.
  • Commands may fail if not referenced by absolute path.
Fixes and example
# Set PATH at top of crontab
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin

# Use absolute path and redirect output
0 2 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /home/user/myscript.py >> /var/log/myscript_cron.log 2>&1
Redirect logs and inspect them to identify missing commands or permission errors quickly.

screens.title: Capturing Output and Avoiding Cron Mail
screens.narratorSegment: Cron will email any output from a job to the account owner by default. On systems with local mail this can quickly fill mailboxes if jobs emit frequent output. The recommended approach is to either redirect output to a log file or to /dev/null when output is not needed. Use the append operator to preserve logs, for example double-greater-than logfile space two-angle ampersand one captures both standard output and standard error. This pattern both archives activity and surfaces errors that need attention. For jobs that must remain silent, send output to /dev/null, but use logging for important maintenance tasks. A concrete example is redirecting both streams to /var/log/my_cron_job. log. A common mistake is to rely on mail delivery to see failures; mail may be disabled or go unread. For troubleshooting, redirect to a log and include timestamps, then inspect the log after the run. You should also implement log rotation for high-volume logs so disk space is not consumed. Which logging strategy will you adopt for routine cron tasks? content.html:
Process Flow

Capturing Output and Avoiding Cron Mail

Redirect output to logs or /dev/null to prevent unwanted mail and to provide actionable error records.

Recommended redirection
* * * * * /bin/echo "$(date) - task" >> /var/log/my_cron_job.log 2>&1
This appends both stdout and stderr, preserving previous runs.
Silencing output
* * * * * /usr/bin/some_quiet_task > /dev/null 2>&1
Use silent mode for tasks that produce no meaningful output and would otherwise create mail noise.
Key Takeaway

Prefer logging with rotation for important jobs and /dev/null for noisy, unimportant ones. Always capture stderr for troubleshooting.

screens.title: Access Control and Safe Script Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Control over who can schedule jobs is an important security consideration. The files cron. allow and cron. deny determine which users can use crontab. If cron. allow exists, only users listed there may use crontab. If cron. allow is absent and cron. deny exists, users listed in cron. deny cannot use crontab. If neither file exists, many distributions allow all users to use crontab, but this can vary, so check your distribution. The at command has similar files: at. allow and at. deny. In addition to allow/deny controls, ensure scripts run by cron or at have correct ownership and permissions. Do not embed secrets or writable temporary files that an attacker could modify. Redirect output to logs and ensure logs are rotated and access controlled. For system-wide scripts, run them as a non-privileged account when possible, or use the username field in /etc/crontab to avoid embedding sudo in scripts. A common mistake is deploying scripts with world-writable permissions or leaving sensitive environment variables in plaintext. By auditing allow/deny files and enforcing strict script permissions you reduce the risk of scheduled tasks becoming attack vectors. Which permission check will you add to your deployment checklist?

Security

Access Control and Safe Script Practices

How allow/deny files control the ability to schedule jobs, and how to protect scripts and logs.

Allow / Deny files
  • cron.allow: If present, only listed users may use crontab.
  • cron.deny: If present and allow absent, listed users are blocked.
  • at uses at.allow and at.deny with similar semantics.
Script hardening
  • Make scripts non-interactive and executable only by intended users.
  • Avoid exposing secrets. Read secrets from secure stores at runtime.
  • Redirect logs to protected locations and rotate them.
Checklist

Verify allow/deny files, check ownership and mode of scripts, and ensure no world-writable temporary files are used.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Create, Verify, and Remove a Cron Job

Follow these terminal steps in a safe environment to practice core workflows.

Step-by-step commands
# Backup existing crontab
$ crontab -l > ~/mycrontab.backup

# Edit crontab
$ crontab -e
# Add this line to the file:
* * * * * /bin/echo "$(date) - My cron job ran!" >> /tmp/my_cron_log.txt 2>&1

# Save and exit. Then verify after one or two minutes:
$ cat /tmp/my_cron_log.txt

# To remove the line, edit again or restore backup:
$ crontab ~/mycrontab.backup
Guidance and checks
  • Use /tmp for disposable test files and logs.
  • If the log is empty, check permissions and absolute paths.
  • Inspect captured logs for 'command not found' to identify PATH issues.
Key Takeaway

Use a backup-edit-verify-restore cycle to manage crontab changes safely and reproducibly.

screens.title: Troubleshoot Common Cron Failures
screens.narratorSegment: When a cron job fails, the most useful data is often in logs or in the redirected output you configured. Start troubleshooting by checking the logfile you directed output to, looking for errors such as command not found, permission denied, or missing files. If the log indicates a missing command, verify the absolute path of the binary on the system and update the crontab line accordingly. If you see permission errors, confirm file and script ownership and modes so the user executing the job can read and execute necessary files. Another useful technique is to run the job command with a non-interactive shell to reproduce the cron environment. For example, run sh -c 'your command' as the target user. Also check the system mail for any cron output if you did not redirect it. Finally, verify daemons are running; if at jobs do not run, confirm atd is active. For persistent problems, add more verbose logging and include environment dumps at the top of your script to compare what cron sees versus your interactive shell. These steps will guide you from surface symptoms to root cause in most cases. What one log entry would immediately point you toward a PATH issue?

content.html:
Troubleshooting

Troubleshoot Common Cron Failures

A recipe to diagnose missing commands, permission issues, and daemon problems.

Stepwise checks
  1. Inspect redirected logfile for error messages.
  2. Run the command as a non-interactive shell to replicate cron.
  3. Verify absolute paths for binaries reported as not found.
  4. Check file and script permissions for the executing user.
  5. Confirm atd or crond are running if jobs do not execute.
Helpful debug commands
# Reproduce cron environment
$ su -s /bin/sh -c '/usr/bin/mytask >> /tmp/mytask.log 2>&1' username

# Check if atd or crond are running
$ systemctl status atd
$ systemctl status crond

# Inspect log for 'command not found' or 'permission denied'
$ tail -n 50 /var/log/my_cron_job.log
Capture environment differences by writing env output at the start of the script and comparing it to your interactive shell.

Automation saves time by running routine work without manual steps. In Linux, cron handles recurring schedules and at covers single future tasks. We also cover the at utility and its queue commands, atq and atrm, so you can schedule one-off jobs. Throughout, we emphasize practical best practices: use absolute paths, redirect output, and verify permissions. A concrete example you will practice is setting a cron job that appends a timestamp to a log file every minute, then removing it safely. Common mistakes include assuming cron inherits your interactive environment and neglecting to capture stdout and stderr, which leads to missed runs or unexpected emails. By the end you will be able to write crontab entries, inspect user and system cron configurations, schedule an at job, and apply secure patterns so scheduled tasks are maintainable. Start troubleshooting by checking the logfile you directed output to, looking for errors such as command not found, permission denied, or missing files. If the log indicates a missing command, verify the absolute path of the binary on the system and update the crontab line accordingly. If you see permission errors, confirm file and script ownership and modes so the user executing the job can read and execute necessary files. Another useful technique is to run the job command with a non-interactive shell to reproduce the cron environment. For example, run sh -c 'your command' as the target user. Also check the system mail for any cron output if you did not redirect it. Finally, verify daemons are running; if at jobs do not run, confirm atd is active. For persistent problems, add more verbose logging and include environment dumps at the top of your script to compare what cron sees versus your interactive shell. These three key concepts summarize the essentials you should retain. First, cron is a time-based scheduler for recurring tasks and relies on crontab files and the cron daemon to run jobs at specified times. Second, crontab syntax uses five fields — minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week — plus commands. Use wildcards, ranges, lists, steps, and special strings like at reboot. Third, the at utility schedules one-time jobs that atd executes; manage these with atq and atrm. Practical habits tie these ideas together: always use absolute paths, set PATH where needed, and redirect output to a log or /dev/null. Control who can schedule jobs with cron. allow and cron. deny and harden scripts with proper permissions. Together these practices make scheduled automation reliable, maintainable, and secure. Keep these concepts close as you write and debug scheduled tasks on your systems.

Here are three practical reminders to carry into your daily administration. First, always use absolute paths and, when helpful, declare PATH at the top of a crontab to avoid 'command not found' errors. Second, redirect both standard output and error to a log file or to /dev/null to control notifications and to provide an audit trail for debugging. Third, manage user access with cron. allow and cron. deny and ensure scripts have appropriate ownership and modes to prevent privilege abuse. These items are operational habits that turn scheduled automation from brittle into reliable. When you write or deploy a scheduled job, confirm the path, set up logging, and validate permissions as your three quick checks. Return to these checks whenever a scheduled job misbehaves and they will often point to the underlying cause.
